newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Labour's first 100 days please right, not left.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Labour's first 100 days please right, not left.

text.p: Three months after taking power, British Prime Minister Tony Blair is being hailed by right-wingers as a paragon of free-market economic virtue but stands accused by some in his own Labour party of abandoning socialism.

Business leaders, who have seen some of their number given key positions in government, clearly like what they see. But the trades unions from which the party sprang view some of Blair's policies with misgivings.

"The government has on the whole exceeded expectations," says Madsen Pirie, president of the Adam Smith Institute, a right-wing think-tank. He has been "agreeably surprised" by the new government's economic policies.

"This a genuinely free-market party. It does seem to be an administration determined to tackle Britain's problems in a constructive way, unencumbered by the narrow class outlook which characterised previous Labour governments. They have now accepted the market and individual choice."

Roy Hattersley, a former deputy Labour leader and government minister, takes a very different view, confessing that the party leadership's abandonment of the socialist belief in equality has made him a "reluctant dissenter" from the new regime.

"Both the manifesto on which Labour was elected and the policies which followed the party's remarkable victory confirm that the hope of equality has been abandoned," Hattersley wrote in a recent newspaper article.

"We should rejoice at the victory of May 1. The Blair government is not only incomparably better than its predecessor. In many ways it is admirable in its own right. But it is not a force for a more equal society."
GORDON BROWN - RADICAL OF CENTRE-LEFT?

Labour Chancellor (finance minister) Gordon Brown established his radical credentials within days of taking office, astounding financial markets by giving the Bank of England the freedom to set interest rates.

But his radicalism has been of the centre-right rather than the left-wing variety. Brown's constant refrain has been that he is determined to build Britain's long-term prosperity and end the damaging cycle of "boom and bust" in which the economy has often appeared trapped.

In his first budget on July 2, Brown kept Labour's election promises, leaving income tax rates unchanged and imposing a "windfall tax" on the profits of privatised utility companies to create jobs for 250,000 unemployed young people.
He also unexpectedly cut corporation tax, although this was intended to sweeten the pill of the abolition of a valuable corporate tax credit on dividend payments.

The government signed the European Social Chapter on workers' rights -- a move opposed by many business leaders who believe it will increase their costs -- but Blair promised it would not be used to impose additional burdens on companies.
There has been virtually no outcry from business.

The government remains committed to a national minimum wage but will await advice from an independent low pay commission. It has left Conservative curbs on local authority spending in place and announced the end of free university education.
LEFT-WING ANGER
Policies such as these have delighted conservatives but angered left-wingers.

Veteran left-wing member of parliament Ken Livingstone, who favours higher corporate and personal taxes to improve public services and reduce government debt, described the budget as "a tragic lost opportunity for Britain."
"Its fundamental errors increase the chance of a mid-term economic crisis and therefore reduce the likelihood of Labour winning a second general election," he said.
Officially, the trade union movement has not ended its honeymoon period with the new government.
Ian Brinkley, an economist at the Trades Union Congress (TUC), says the government has tried to take a neutral role between employers and unions.

"So far we think the government is doing pretty well," he says. "The chancellor has signalled his interest in developing long-term strategies on employment and investment. You could hardly describe the windfall tax as a pro-employer measure but the unions haven't got everything they wanted either. It is pretty clear that the government is not going to be in hock to the unions, it's going to steer a middle course."
Some union leaders, who maintained a diplomatic low profile in the run-up to the election, are concerned about Labour's drift away from its roots in the industrial working-class.

"Manufacturing is something very few MPs -- and very few New Labour adminstrators -- understand," complained Ken Jackson, general secretary of the Amalgamated Engineering and Electrical Union. "Despite changes in the spread of business in Britain today, it is still manufacturing that creates the wealth which funds our schools, hospitals and welfare services."
Jackson warned the Labour leadership against loosening links with the unions even further, as it appears likely to do.

"If the unions' link with Labour is broken, New Labour would, I'm afraid, become the preserve of those who inhabit the worlds of the media, courts and academia," he wrote in the Independent newspaper.

David Marquand, principal of Mansfield College, Oxford, sees "an unacknowledged tension" between the conservatism of New Labour's economics and the radicalism of its politics, as expressed in its ambitious plans for constitutional reform.

"Despite their nods towards the Social Chapter and the minimum wage, today's Blairites, like yesterday's Thatcherites, evidently believe that Britain should seek competitive advantage in the global market-place through low non-wage labour costs, correspondingly low levels of social protection and deregulated labour markets," he wrote in the Guardian newspaper.
Marquand also sees tensions within the psyche of the prime minister.

"Plainly, he is a radical. As plainly, he is also a conservative. He is a child of the 1960s, who is also a child of the 1980s; a participative democrat who has imposed a Prussian discipline on his own party."
Blair has undoubtedly been lucky in inheriting a fairly healthy economy, with steady growth, falling unemployment and inflation under control.
"Sooner or later, however, there will be a time of trouble," Marquand says. "Only then will we find out what he and his government are made of."
